newsitem.title: UK: On LIFFE, British election eclipsed by EMU worries.
newsitem.headline: On LIFFE, British election eclipsed by EMU worries.

text.p: The announcement of an election in Britain normally generates lively trading in financial markets, but for many dealers on LIFFE the emphasis has shifted away from the narrow focus of British politics.
A muted reaction to news on Monday Britain will have an election on May 1 was easily drowned out by concerns about European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), traders said.
"Gilts didn't really start moving until the Bund hit key technical levels," said a broker at a British bank in London.
"As far as the market is concerned, there's not much to choose between Labour and the Conservatives on economic policy," the broker said. "It's EMU that's the market-mover."

Although interest rate and debt futures on LIFFE see-sawed as Prime Minister John Major set the election date, bigger movements during the session were inspired by weakness in Bunds and the wider issue of the timetable for EMU.

British June gilt futures were down 25/32 at 110-12 by 1515 GMT, while short sterling futures were off six basis points at 93.51. Most of that followed a decline ins June Bund futures, which fell 0.77 at 100.66.
"Once Bunds dropped through 100.82, it was a sell from a technical view," said a trader at a German house. "EMU, and whether there is likely to be a delay, is the major story."
Earlier, German finance minister Theo Waigel said meeting the economic targets for membership took precedence over the timetable, but he also said special factors can be taken into account.
A spokesman for the German opposition SPD said Bonn did not stand a chance of meeting the criteria in time for the proposed launch date of January 1, 1999.
Traders pointed out that there has been little sign of investors hedging against a victory by Labour -- even though it would mean the end of the status quo which has been in place since 1979.
"Last election we saw lots of call spreads and put spreads trading, but not now," said the head of options at a German firm.

The relative calm in the market was a far cry from the last time Labour had a fighting chance of getting into power. Implied volatility of short sterling options rose to 50 percent prior to the 1992 British election, which compares with just 10 percent for June short sterling options on Monday.
"There just isn't the investor worry about Labour that there was," the options head said, adding that short sterling volatility was unlikely to break above 15 percent.

According to an NOP opinion poll published on Sunday, the Labour Party has extended its lead by seven points to 52 percent of the vote, compared with a fall of four points to 27 percent for the Conservatives.

Brokers attributed the growing acceptance of Labour as a market-friendly party to Labour economics spokesman Gordon Brown. Brown -- who is likely to be the next finance minister if opinion polls are correct and Labour comes to power -- has already promised to freeze income tax rates and to keep public spending in check for the next two years.
Britain's opposition leader, Tony Blair, underlined the message, saying his party had changed for good and there would be no return to the days of a much more left-wing "Old Labour."
"The expectation here is of a seamless change of power," said the options head. "There was a smooth change from Republicans to Democrats in the U.S., why not here?"
